items.followUp: Define any four branches of chemistry other than those named in your answer.

rubric.why: Physical chemistry deals with physical properties and changes of matter.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying physical properties or changes of matter as its subject.

rubric.why: Organic chemistry is the study of carbon compounds.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying carbon compounds as its subject.

rubric.why: Inorganic chemistry studies elements and their compounds, generally excluding most carbon compounds.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying elements and their compounds as its subject.

rubric.why: Analytical chemistry identifies substances and determines their composition.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying substances or determining their composition as its subject.

modelAnswer: Physical chemistry deals with the physical properties and changes of matter and the energy changes involved.
Organic chemistry is the study of carbon compounds.
Inorganic chemistry is the study of elements and their compounds, generally excluding most carbon compounds.
Analytical chemistry deals with identifying substances and determining their composition.

items.followUp: Explain ionic bonding and describe two types of covalent bonds with examples.

rubric.why: A covalent bond forms when atoms share electrons.
rubric.description: States that a covalent bond forms by sharing electrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that electrons are shared.

rubric.why: The electrons shared in a covalent bond form one or more pairs.
rubric.description: States that the shared electrons form pairs.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the shared electrons form one or more pairs.

rubric.why: A single covalent bond has one shared pair; H₂ is an example.
rubric.description: Describes a single covalent bond and gives an example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying one shared pair and giving a suitable example such as H₂.

rubric.why: A double covalent bond has two shared pairs; O₂ is an example.
rubric.description: Describes a double covalent bond and gives an example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying two shared pairs and giving a suitable example such as O₂.

rubric.why: A triple covalent bond has three shared pairs; N₂ is an example.
rubric.description: Describes a triple covalent bond and gives an example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying three shared pairs and giving a suitable example such as N₂.

modelAnswer: A covalent bond is formed when two atoms share one or more pairs of electrons.
A single covalent bond has one shared pair of electrons; for example, hydrogen (H₂).
A double covalent bond has two shared pairs of electrons; for example, oxygen (O₂).
A triple covalent bond has three shared pairs of electrons; for example, nitrogen (N₂).

items.followUp: Define crystalline and amorphous solids and give one example of each.

rubric.why: Crystalline solids have particles arranged in a regular, orderly pattern.
rubric.description: Describes the particle arrangement in a crystalline solid.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the particles have a regular or orderly arrangement.

rubric.why: Sodium chloride is an example of a crystalline solid.
rubric.description: Gives an example of a crystalline solid.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a suitable example such as sodium chloride or quartz.

rubric.why: Amorphous solids do not have a regular arrangement of particles.
rubric.description: Describes the particle arrangement in an amorphous solid.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the particles lack a regular arrangement.

rubric.why: Glass is an example of an amorphous solid.
rubric.description: Gives an example of an amorphous solid.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a suitable example such as glass, plastic, rubber or wax.

modelAnswer: Crystalline solids have particles arranged in a regular, orderly pattern; sodium chloride (NaCl) is an example.
Amorphous solids do not have a regular arrangement of particles; glass is an example.
